Based on your lecture notes, the topics we are exploring are 

RISC vs CISC

, 

Computer Organization vs Computer Architecture

, 

Instruction Set (ISA)

, and 

MIPS Architecture

.

Here are clear, concise definitions for each of these topics, researched from authoritative web sources:

1. 

RISC vs CISC

RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer)

: A processor design philosophy focusing on a small, simplified set of highly optimized, fixed-length instructions. Because each instruction typically executes in a single clock cycle, RISC offers fast execution and high power efficiency, making it the standard for mobile and embedded devices (such as ARM processors).

CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer)

: A processor design philosophy that uses a larger set of complex, variable-length instructions. A single CISC instruction can perform multiple operations (e.g., loading data from memory, executing an arithmetic calculation, and saving it back), which reduces the number of instructions per program but requires more complex hardware and multiple clock cycles per instruction (standard in Intel/AMD x86 desktop processors).

2. 

Computer Organization vs. Computer Architecture

Computer Architecture

: The conceptual design and functional blueprint of a computer system from the programmer's point of view (the 

"what"

 of a computer). It defines what the processor can do, specifying features like the instruction set architecture (ISA), data types, and addressing modes.

Computer Organization

: The physical implementation and concrete realization of the architecture (the 

"how"

 of a computer). It specifies how the underlying hardware components—such as registers, control units, arithmetic logic units (ALUs), and buses—are physically structured and interconnected to meet the architectural specifications.

3. 

Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)

Definition

: The abstract boundary and programmable interface between a computer's software and hardware. The ISA defines the complete set of commands (instructions) that a processor is designed to understand and execute—such as arithmetic operations, data movement, and control flow—along with the registers, addressing modes, and memory models available to programmers and compilers.

4. 

MIPS Architecture

Definition

: A classic RISC instruction set architecture (ISA) designed by MIPS Computer Systems (standing for 

Microprocessor without Interlocked Pipeline Stages

). It features a clean, highly regular instruction set, fixed-length instructions, and a load-store memory model. Due to its simplicity, it is widely used as a foundational teaching model in computer architecture courses and continues to power various embedded systems.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


Here's what I found on 

computer architecture fundamentals

:

I found that the division between high-level instruction set interfaces and low-level physical implementation is central to microprocessor design, with architectures like MIPS exemplifying the streamlined, regular execution typical of RISC-based systems.

Key themes I noticed:

Abstraction and Implementation Boundary

: ISAs act as the definitive contract between compilers/software developers and the hardware implementation.

Design Tradeoffs in Instruction Complexity

: RISC and CISC represent competing strategies to optimize CPU execution speed, either by making hardware simpler (RISC) or by making instructions more expressive (CISC).

MIPS as a Pedagogical Benchmark

: Due to its highly systematic RISC structure, MIPS remains the preeminent architecture for demonstrating pipeline stages and register-transfer operations.

{"status":"success","content":"The PCIe Architecture

In Chapter 3, 

PCI Express (PCIe)

 is introduced as a major evolutionary milestone in computer system interconnections. To understand PCIe fully, it helps to look at why computer architectures shifted away from traditional shared buses toward modern 

point-to-point interconnects

.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


1. The Larger Context: The Shift to Point-to-Point Interconnects

Historically, computers relied on 

shared, broadcast buses

 (such as standard PCI or Unibus) to connect the CPU, main memory, and peripheral devices. However, as processor clock speeds and bandwidth demands surged, traditional shared buses hit severe physical and performance bottlenecks:

Electrical Constraints

: At higher frequencies, wide synchronous shared buses suffer from propagation delays and signal coordination difficulties across long physical traces.

Arbitration Overhead

: Because only one device can control a shared bus at a time, devices must continually request and wait for bus control.

Scalability Bottlenecks

: As multi-core processors emerged, sharing a single bus among multiple cores and high-speed peripherals severely choked data throughput.

To resolve these issues, computer architectures moved to 

point-to-point interconnects

 like PCIe and Intel's QuickPath Interconnect (QPI). Instead of sharing a central bus, devices connect via dedicated direct links, delivering 

lower latency, higher data throughput, and vastly superior scalability

.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


2. Overview and Role of PCI Express (PCIe)

Developed and maintained by the 

PCI Special Interest Group (SIG)

, PCIe is a point-to-point interconnect scheme engineered to replace older bus-based standards like PCI. Its primary goal is to provide high capacity and throughput for data-intensive I/O devices (such as Gigabit Ethernet controllers and high-performance graphics cards) and to support time-dependent data streams.

In a typical PCIe system configuration:

A central 

chipset

 links processor cores to memory and root PCIe lanes.

PCIe Switches

 act as traffic routers, fanning out connections to multiple PCIe endpoints, legacy PCI bridges, or expansion slots.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


3. The PCIe Layered Protocol Architecture

Rather than relying on basic control lines like traditional buses, PCIe uses a 

layered protocol architecture

 consisting of three distinct layers:

A. Physical Layer

Lanes & Signaling

: Operates using point-to-point 

bidirectional lanes

 (a port can feature 1, 4, 8, 16, or 32 lanes). Data bytes are distributed across these lanes in a round-robin fashion.

Block Encoding

: Data is processed in 16-byte (128-bit) blocks and encoded into 

130-bit code words

 (128b/130b encoding) for physical transmission.

Self-Clocking

: There is 

no common shared clock

 signal across devices. Instead, the receiver synchronizes its clock by detecting voltage transitions directly in the data stream; the extra 2 encoding bits guarantee sufficient transitions even during long strings of 

1

s or 

0

s.

B. Data Link Layer

Packet Handling

: Converts data into 

Data Link Layer Packets (DLLPs)

 and handles error checking and address validation.

Flow & Power Control

: Regulates the rate at which packets are transmitted to prevent buffer overflows and manages platform power budgeting.

Reliability (ACK/NAK)

: Uses 

ACK

 (acknowledgement) for successfully received packets and 

NAK

 (negative acknowledgement) to request retransmission of corrupted packets.

C. Transaction Layer (TL)

Request Processing

: Receives read and write requests from software and formats them into 

Transaction Layer Packets (TLPs)

.

Split Transactions

: Employs a 

split transaction technique

, where a source device issues a request packet and frees up the link while waiting for a completion response from the target device.

Posted Transactions

: Certain write operations and messages are 

posted

, meaning no response packet is expected.

Addressing

: Fully supports both 

32-bit memory addressing

 and extended 

64-bit memory addressing

.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


🎯 

Next Steps

: Would you like to explore how PCIe compares to 

Intel's QuickPath Interconnect (QPI)

 in multicore setups, or solve a bus timing problem from Chapter 3?","title":"The PCIe Architecture","source_type":"unknown","char_count":4544}

# Fundamentals of Computer Architecture and MIPS Design

Source: NotebookLM source "Session 31/08". Topics: RISC vs CISC, Computer Organization vs Architecture, ISA, MIPS.

## 1. RISC vs CISC

- **RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer)**: a small, simplified set of highly optimized, fixed-length instructions. Each instruction typically executes in one clock cycle, giving fast execution and high power efficiency. Standard in mobile and embedded devices (e.g. ARM).
- **CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer)**: a larger set of complex, variable-length instructions. One instruction can do several operations (load from memory, compute, store back), so programs need fewer instructions, but the hardware is more complex and instructions take multiple cycles. Standard in Intel/AMD x86.

## 2. Computer Organization vs Computer Architecture

- **Architecture**: the conceptual design and functional blueprint from the programmer's point of view, the "what". It defines what the processor can do: the ISA, data types, addressing modes.
- **Organization**: the physical implementation of the architecture, the "how". Registers, control units, ALUs, and buses, and how they are structured and interconnected.

## 3. Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)

The abstract boundary and programmable interface between software and hardware. It defines the complete set of instructions a processor understands (arithmetic, data movement, control flow) along with the registers, addressing modes, and memory models available to programmers and compilers.

## 4. MIPS Architecture

A classic RISC ISA from MIPS Computer Systems (Microprocessor without Interlocked Pipeline Stages). Clean, highly regular instruction set, fixed-length instructions, load-store memory model. Widely used as a teaching model.

## Key themes

- **Abstraction boundary**: the ISA is the contract between compilers/software and the hardware implementation.
- **Instruction complexity tradeoff**: RISC simplifies hardware; CISC makes instructions more expressive.
- **MIPS as benchmark**: its systematic RISC structure suits demonstrating pipeline stages and register-transfer operations.

- **RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer)**: a small, simplified set of highly optimized, fixed-length instructions. Each instruction typically executes in one clock cycle, giving fast execution and high power efficiency. Standard in mobile and embedded devices (e.g. ARM).
- **CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer)**: a larger set of complex, variable-length instructions. One instruction can do several operations (load from memory, compute, store back), so programs need fewer instructions, but the hardware is more complex and instructions take multiple cycles. Standard in Intel/AMD x86.

## 2. Computer Organization vs Computer Architecture

- **Architecture**: the conceptual design and functional blueprint from the programmer's point of view, the "what". It defines what the processor can do: the ISA, data types, addressing modes.
- **Organization**: the physical implementation of the architecture, the "how". Registers, control units, ALUs, and buses, and how they are structured and interconnected.

## 3. Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)

The abstract boundary and programmable interface between software and hardware. It defines the complete set of instructions a processor understands (arithmetic, data movement, control flow) along with the registers, addressing modes, and memory models available to programmers and compilers.

## 4. MIPS Architecture

A classic RISC ISA from MIPS Computer Systems (Microprocessor without Interlocked Pipeline Stages). Clean, highly regular instruction set, fixed-length instructions, load-store memory model. Widely used as a teaching model.

## Key themes

- **Abstraction boundary**: the ISA is the contract between compilers/software and the hardware implementation.
- **Instruction complexity tradeoff**: RISC simplifies hardware; CISC makes instructions more expressive.
- **MIPS as benchmark**: its systematic RISC structure suits demonstrating pipeline stages and register-transfer operations.

# The PCIe Architecture

Source: NotebookLM source "The PCIe Architecture" (Chapter 3).

## 1. Shift to point-to-point interconnects

Historically, computers used shared, broadcast buses (standard PCI, Unibus) to connect CPU, memory, and peripherals. As clock speeds and bandwidth demands rose, these hit limits:

- **Electrical constraints**: at high frequencies, wide synchronous shared buses suffer propagation delays and signal coordination problems over long traces.
- **Arbitration overhead**: only one device controls a shared bus at a time, so devices must request and wait.
- **Scalability**: multi-core processors and fast peripherals sharing one bus choke throughput.

The fix was point-to-point interconnects like PCIe and Intel QuickPath Interconnect (QPI): dedicated direct links with lower latency, higher throughput, and better scalability.

## 2. Overview and role of PCIe

Developed by the PCI Special Interest Group (SIG), PCIe is a point-to-point interconnect meant to replace bus-based standards like PCI. Goal: high capacity and throughput for data-intensive I/O (Gigabit Ethernet, high-performance graphics) and support for time-dependent data streams.

Typical configuration:

- A central **chipset** links processor cores to memory and root PCIe lanes.
- **PCIe switches** route traffic, fanning out to multiple endpoints, legacy PCI bridges, or expansion slots.

## 3. Layered protocol architecture

### Physical layer

- **Lanes**: point-to-point bidirectional lanes; a port can have 1, 4, 8, 16, or 32 lanes. Bytes are distributed across lanes round-robin.
- **Block encoding**: 16-byte (128-bit) blocks encoded into 130-bit code words (128b/130b).
- **Self-clocking**: no common shared clock. The receiver syncs by detecting voltage transitions in the data stream; the 2 extra encoding bits guarantee enough transitions even during long runs of 1s or 0s.

### Data link layer

- **Packets**: converts data into Data Link Layer Packets (DLLPs); handles error checking and address validation.
- **Flow and power control**: regulates packet rate to prevent buffer overflow; manages platform power budgeting.
- **Reliability**: ACK for successfully received packets, NAK to request retransmission of corrupted ones.

### Transaction layer (TL)

- **Requests**: takes read/write requests from software and formats them into Transaction Layer Packets (TLPs).
- **Split transactions**: the source issues a request and frees the link while waiting for the target's completion response.
- **Posted transactions**: some writes and messages are posted, meaning no response packet is expected.
- **Addressing**: supports 32-bit and extended 64-bit memory addressing.

## Next steps

Compare PCIe with Intel QPI in multicore setups, or solve a bus timing problem from Chapter 3.

# Chapter 1: Basic Concepts & Computer Evolution

Slides: `Attachments/Chapter 1 - Basic Concepts & Computer Evolution.pdf`. Stallings, *Computer Organization and Architecture*, 11th Global Ed. Next: [[Chapter 2 - Performance Issues]]. All chapters together: [[Cross-Chapter Connections]].

## The one idea

A computer is a small set of components (CPU, memory, I/O, interconnect) doing four things (process, store, move data, control), and the whole history in this chapter is the same design being rebuilt with smaller, faster, cheaper parts while the programmer-visible interface stays put. The stored-program concept (von Neumann) is the hinge: program and data sit in the same memory, so changing behaviour means changing memory contents, not rewiring.

## Architecture vs organization vs ISA

- **Architecture**: attributes visible to the programmer. Instruction set, data representation widths, I/O mechanisms, addressing modes. Example question: is there a multiply instruction?
- **Organization**: how those features are implemented. Control signals, interfaces, memory technology. Example question: is there a hardware multiplier, or is multiply done by repeated addition?
- **ISA**: the interface between hardware and the lowest-level software; everything a programmer needs to write a correct binary program (instructions, registers, memory access, I/O). It lets designers talk about function independently of hardware, like describing a digital clock's functions without mentioning the quartz crystal.
- **Families**: one architecture, many organizations. The IBM System/370 family keeps code compatibility (at least backwards) while models differ in price and performance. This is why the architecture/organization split matters commercially.

Session 31/08 phrasing that is easy to remember: architecture is the "what", organization is the "how".

## Structure and function

- **Functions**: data processing, data storage, data movement, control.
- **Top-level structure** (single processor): CPU, main memory, I/O, system interconnection.
- **Inside the CPU**: control unit, ALU, registers, CPU-internal interconnection.
- **Multicore**: several processing units on one chip; each unit (control unit, ALU, registers, cache) is a core.

## ENIAC (1943–46)

First general-purpose electronic digital computer (Eckert and Mauchly, U Penn). Built for artillery trajectory tables, finished too late for the war, then used for hydrogen bomb feasibility calculations until 1955. Decimal, not binary; 20 accumulators of 10 digits; programmed manually by switches; 18,000 vacuum tubes, 30 tons, 1,500 sq ft, 140 kW, 5,000 additions/s. Its weakness is the reason for von Neumann: rewiring/re-switching is the program.

## Von Neumann / IAS (designed 1946, completed 1952)

Stored-program concept: main memory holds programs and data; ALU works on binary data; control unit interprets instructions from memory; I/O is run by the control unit.

**IAS specifics**

- Memory: 4096 words × 40 bits. 4096 = $2^{12}$, so addresses are 12 bits.
- Each 40-bit word holds either one number or **two 20-bit instructions**. A 20-bit instruction is an 8-bit opcode plus a 12-bit address (8 + 12 = 20).

**IAS registers**

| Register | Job |
|---|---|
| MBR (memory buffer) | word going to/from memory or I/O |
| MAR (memory address) | address in memory for the MBR transfer |
| IR (instruction) | the 8-bit opcode being executed |
| IBR (instruction buffer) | temporarily holds the right-hand instruction of a fetched word |
| PC (program counter) | address of the next instruction *pair* to fetch |
| AC and MQ | operands and results of ALU operations (multiply/divide use both) |

The IBR exists because one fetch brings in two instructions; the right-hand one waits there so the next cycle needs no memory access.

### Worked IAS problems from the slides

- **1.2a**: store AC to address 8 → `STOR M(8)`. **1.2b**: add memory 16 to AC → `ADD M(16)`.
- **1.4**: memory at 08A–08C is `010FA210FB`, `010FA0F08D`, `020FA210FB`. Splitting each word into 20-bit halves (opcode 8 bits + address 12 bits):

```
08A left : 01 0FA  LOAD M(0FA)
08A right: 21 0FB  STOR M(0FB)
08B left : 01 0FA  LOAD M(0FA)
08B right: 0F 08D  JUMP+ M(08D,0:19)
08C left : 02 0FA  LOAD -M(0FA)
08C right: 21 0FB  STOR M(0FB)
```

  Result: M(0FB) = |M(0FA)| (absolute value), matching the slide's answer. The slide's solution text is the only thing I could verify; the opcode names come from the IAS instruction set table (an image on slide 18), so double check them there.

### Class exercise (from your notes): `if (M(5) > 0) then M(6) = M(7) + M(8)`

Sequence in your notes:

```
LOAD  M(5)
JUMP+ M(1,0:19)
LOAD  M(7)
ADD   M(8)
STOR  M(6)
```

Worth re-checking against what the lecturer wrote: `JUMP+` jumps when AC ≥ 0, so as written the jump is taken when M(5) is positive, which would skip the addition in exactly the case where it should run. A version that skips when M(5) ≤ 0 is `LOAD -M(5)` then `JUMP+ <skip target>` (−M(5) ≥ 0 exactly when M(5) ≤ 0), followed by the load/add/store. I can't tell from the notes whether the lecturer's target address and layout make the original correct, so treat this as a flag, not a verdict.

## History in one pass

**Generations** (driven by the switching technology): vacuum tubes → transistors → integrated circuits (dozens to hundreds of transistors per chip) → VLSI (billions of switches in one package).

| Year | Milestone | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1947 | Transistor (Bell Labs, Shockley et al.) | electrically controlled on/off switch; smaller, cheaper, cooler than tubes; silicon |
| 1947–50 | UNIVAC I (Eckert-Mauchly) | first commercial computer; 1950 US Census |
| 1953 / 1955 | IBM 701 / 702 | first IBM stored-program machine (scientific) / business use; led to 700/7000 series |
| 1957 | DEC PDP-1 | transistor era, DEC's first |
| 1964 | IBM System/360 | first planned family: similar instruction sets and OS, rising speed, I/O ports, memory, and cost; not compatible with 7000 series |
| 1964 | DEC PDP-8 | first minicomputer; $16,000 vs $100k+ for a 360; Omnibus bus structure |
| 1970 | Fairchild semiconductor memory | 256 bits on a chip the size of one magnetic core; much faster, capacity roughly doubling each year |
| 1971 / 72 / 74 | Intel 4004 / 8008 / 8080 | first microprocessor (4-bit) / 8-bit / first general-purpose |

The PDP-8 Omnibus matters later: it is the shared-bus idea that [[Chapter 3 - Function and Interconnection]] spends most of its time on.

## Moore's Law

Gordon Moore (Intel co-founder): transistors per chip double every year in the original statement, roughly every 18 months since the 1970s (the slide states both). Chip cost stays about flat. Consequences: shorter electrical paths (higher performance), smaller size (more flexibility), less power and cooling, fewer interconnections (more reliability).

## CISC vs RISC

- **CISC** (x86): large set of complex, variable-length instructions; one instruction can do load + compute + store; fewer instructions per program, more cycles each, more complex hardware.
- **RISC** (ARM, MIPS): small set of simple, fixed-length instructions, roughly one cycle each, load-store memory model, power efficient.
- Slide example, `A = B + C`. CISC: `add mem(A), mem(B), mem(C)` (1 instruction). RISC: `load B→r1`, `load C→r2`, `add r1,r1,r2`, `store r1→A` (4 instructions).
- **MIPS the architecture** (Microprocessor without Interlocked Pipeline Stages): clean, regular RISC ISA used as the teaching model. Not the same thing as the MIPS *metric* in [[Chapter 2 - Performance Issues]].

## Intel x86 evolution

| Chip | Headline feature |
|---|---|
| 8080 | first general-purpose µP; 8-bit data path; first PC (Altair) |
| 8086 | 16-bit; instruction cache, prefetch; 8088 variant with 8-bit external bus in the first IBM PC |
| 80286 | 16 MB addressable (up from 1 MB) |
| 80386 | 32-bit, multitasking support |
| 80486 | cache and instruction pipelining, built-in math coprocessor |
| Pentium | superscalar: multiple instructions in parallel |
| Pentium Pro | more superscalar, register renaming, branch prediction, data flow analysis, speculative execution |
| Pentium II / III / 4 | MMX (media), 3D floating-point instructions, more FP/multimedia |
| Core / Core 2 | dual core; 64-bit; Core 2 Quad; later up to 10 cores; 256/512-bit vector instructions |

The pattern to notice: after the 486, almost every gain is a *performance technique* (pipelining, superscalar, prediction, speculation, multicore), which is exactly the list that opens [[Chapter 2 - Performance Issues]].

## Embedded systems, microcontrollers, ARM, cloud

- **Embedded system**: a computer inside another device running one predetermined application (car, TV, airplane, cargo ship). The processor only needs to be as fast as the function requires; cost and power matter most; failure tolerance is low, and dependability comes from simplicity. Differs from a PC by its many interfaces to the physical world, a diagnostic port for the *controlled* system, and possible FPGA/ASIC/non-digital hardware for speed or safety.
- **Microprocessor vs microcontroller**: a microcontroller is one chip with processor, ROM (program), RAM (I/O data), clock, and I/O control unit; the processor part has far smaller silicon area and much better energy efficiency.
- **ARM**: RISC microprocessors and microcontrollers; the company designs and licenses architectures rather than making chips; high speed, small die, low power; 32-bit instructions; phones, handhelds, consumer products.
- **Cloud**: warehouse-scale computers (around 100,000 servers) rented out. **SaaS** delivers software, **PaaS** a platform for your applications, **IaaS** processing, storage, and networks.

## Check yourself

- Why does the IAS need an IBR? Why is PC "the next instruction *pair*"?
- Give one architecture question and one organization question about multiplication.
- What did System/360 introduce that the 7000 series lacked?
- For `A = B + C`, which style has the lower instruction count, and which has the lower CPI? (This sets up [[Cross-Chapter Connections]].)

# Chapter 2: Performance Issues

Slides: `Attachments/Chapter 2 - Performance Issues.pdf`. Sources: Stallings 11e and Patterson & Hennessy, *Computer Organization and Design*, 5e. Previous: [[Chapter 1 - Basic Concepts & Computer Evolution]]. Next: [[Chapter 3 - Function and Interconnection]]. All chapters together: [[Cross-Chapter Connections]].

**Class status**: the lecture stopped at slide 7 (see the note on 4G, IoT, DMA, "cache is king" below); slides 8 onward are self-study so far.

## The one idea

Speed comes from two places, faster hardware and smarter organization, and both are now hitting walls (power, wire delay, memory latency). The rest of the chapter gives you the tool to argue about performance properly: **execution time** is the only real measure, and it factors into instruction count × CPI × cycle time. Amdahl's Law then caps what any single improvement can achieve.

## Why performance keeps rising

Cost drops while performance and capacity climb; a laptop now has the power of a mainframe from 10–15 years ago. Applications this enabled: engine control and safety in cars, mobile phones, the human genome project (equipment cost fell from hundreds of millions of dollars), search engines. Your class notes add that AI is now a major demand driver, and that telecom went from fixed hardware to software-enabled networking starting with 4G (IoT, Wi-Fi calling offload, Web 2.0 dynamic content).

## Techniques for speeding up

Pipelining, on-board cache, branch prediction, superscalar execution, data flow analysis, speculative execution. (These are the same features [[Chapter 1 - Basic Concepts & Computer Evolution]] lists for Pentium through Pentium Pro.)

## The memory bottleneck

Processor speed and memory capacity grew, but memory *speed* lags processor speed. Your note's analogy: an ultra-fast CPU on slow memory is a Ferrari on a mountain road. The bottleneck has moved from processing speed to data movement.

Fixes from the slides:

- Retrieve more bits at once: make DRAM wider rather than deeper, change the DRAM interface, put cache on the DRAM chip.
- Reduce the frequency of memory accesses: more complex cache, cache on the processor chip. "Cache is King" in your notes.
- Increase interconnection bandwidth: high-speed buses, a hierarchy of buses. (This is the bridge into [[Chapter 3 - Function and Interconnection]].)
- DMA, from your notes: memory and peripherals exchange data without burdening the CPU. Detail in Chapter 3.

## Hardware improvements and their limits

Gains from shrinking gates (more gates packed tighter, shorter propagation), raising clock rate, and bigger/faster caches, plus organizational changes for parallel instruction execution. Limits:

- **Power** rises with clock rate and density.
- **RC delay**: as components shrink, wires get thinner (R up) and closer together (C up), so the RC product and delay go up.
- **Memory latency and throughput** stay behind.

The response is parallelism on the chip instead of a faster clock:

- **Multicore**: several processors on one chip with a large shared cache; more performance without raising the clock.
- **MIC** (Many Integrated Cores): 50+ cores per chip.
- **GPGPU**: the same operation on many data sets at once.

## Measuring performance

- **Response (execution) time**: start to finish of a task; what a PC user cares about.
- **Throughput**: total work per unit time; what a datacenter manager cares about.
- Maximize performance = minimize execution time: $\text{Performance} = \dfrac{1}{\text{Execution time}}$. "X is $n$ times as fast as Y" means $\dfrac{\text{Perf}_X}{\text{Perf}_Y} = \dfrac{\text{Time}_Y}{\text{Time}_X} = n$.
- Example: A takes 10 s, B takes 15 s → A is $15/10 = 1.5$ times as fast as B.
- **Wall-clock / elapsed time** includes disk, memory, I/O, and OS overhead. **CPU time** counts only the time the CPU spends computing for this task, excluding I/O waits and other programs.
- **Clock cycle** = one discrete tick; clock period (e.g. 250 ps) and clock rate (e.g. 4 GHz) are inverses.

## The CPU performance equation

$$\text{CPU time} = \text{IC} \times \text{CPI} \times T_{\text{cycle}} = \frac{\text{IC} \times \text{CPI}}{\text{clock rate}}$$

- **IC**: instructions executed (measured with software tools, simulators, hardware counters).
- **CPI**: average clock cycles per instruction (hardware counters).
- **$T_{\text{cycle}}$**: seconds per clock cycle (from documentation).
- Also $\text{CPU time} = \dfrac{\text{clock cycles}}{\text{clock rate}}$, so performance improves by reducing cycles or raising clock rate.
- **Weighted CPI** when instruction classes differ: $\text{CPI} = \sum_i \text{CPI}_i \times \dfrac{\text{IC}_i}{\text{IC}}$, with $\text{Cycles} = \sum_i \text{CPI}_i \times \text{IC}_i$.

### Worked examples (slides show the setup; answers here are my working)

**Clock rate target** (slides 17–18): A runs the program in 10 s at 2 GHz → $10 \times 2\times10^9 = 20\times10^9$ cycles. B must finish in 6 s using $1.2 \times 20\times10^9 = 24\times10^9$ cycles → clock rate $= 24\times10^9 / 6 = 4$ GHz.

**Two implementations of one ISA** (slides 20–21): same instruction count $I$. A: $I \times 2.0 \times 250\text{ ps} = 500 I$ ps. B: $I \times 1.2 \times 500\text{ ps} = 600 I$ ps. A is faster by $600/500 = 1.2$. Lower CPI on B did not win because B's cycle time is twice as long.

**Comparing code sequences** (slides 24–25), CPI per class A/B/C = 1/2/3:

| Sequence | Instructions (A, B, C) | Total instructions | Cycles | CPI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2, 1, 2 | 5 | $2{\cdot}1 + 1{\cdot}2 + 2{\cdot}3 = 10$ | 2.0 |
| 2 | 4, 1, 1 | 6 | $4{\cdot}1 + 1{\cdot}2 + 1{\cdot}3 = 9$ | 1.5 |

Sequence 2 executes *more* instructions but fewer cycles, so it is faster. Instruction count alone misleads.

## MIPS and MFLOPS (the metrics, and their pitfall)

$$\text{MIPS rate} = \frac{\text{IC}}{\text{time} \times 10^6} = \frac{\text{clock rate}}{\text{CPI} \times 10^6} \qquad \text{MFLOPS} = \frac{\text{FP operations}}{\text{time} \times 10^6}$$

Pitfall from the slides: using a subset of the performance equation as a metric. Execution time is the only valid measure.

**Slide example**: 2 million instructions on a 400 MHz processor.

| Type | CPI | Mix |
|---|---|---|
| Arithmetic/logic | 1 | 60% |
| Load/store, cache hit | 2 | 18% |
| Branch | 4 | 12% |
| Memory reference, cache miss | 8 | 10% |

Average CPI = $0.6 + 0.36 + 0.48 + 0.8 = 2.24$; MIPS = $400/2.24 \approx 178$. Execution time would be $2\times10^6 \times 2.24 / 400\times10^6 = 11.2$ ms (my arithmetic, not on the slide).

Note the cache-miss row: 10% of instructions cost 8 cycles each, 0.8 of the 2.24 total CPI, so memory behaviour is over a third of the CPI. That is the memory bottleneck showing up in the equation.

## Amdahl's Law

Performance gain from an improvement is limited by how much the improved part is used.

$$T_{\text{new}} = \frac{T_{\text{affected}}}{n} + T_{\text{unaffected}} \qquad \text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + \dfrac{f}{N}}$$

$f$ is the fraction that benefits from the improvement, $N$ the improvement factor (cores, or module speedup $K$).

- **Motivating example**: a program takes 100 s, of which 20 s (directory scan, P1) is sequential and 80 s (P2) parallelizable. With 2 units: $80/2 + 20 = 60$ s.
- **Five times faster?** Needs 20 s total: $80/n + 20 = 20 \Rightarrow 80/n = 0$, impossible for any finite $n$. Even infinite processors give at most $100/20 = 5\times$ at $n\to\infty$, never reached with finite resources.
- **FP example**: 40% of time is floating point, module sped up by $K$: $\text{Speedup} = \dfrac{1}{0.6 + 0.4/K}$. As $K\to\infty$ it approaches $1/0.6 \approx 1.67$.

## Benchmarks and SPEC

Benchmarks summarize performance on realistic code. Good ones are written in a high-level language (portable), representative of a programming style, easy to measure, and widely distributed. **SPEC** is an industry consortium maintaining benchmark suites. **SPEC CPU2017**: the standard for processor-intensive work (compute-heavy rather than I/O-heavy), from real applications rather than synthetic loops; 23 floating-point and 20 integer programs in C, C++, Fortran; 11+ million lines of code; sixth generation after CPU2006.

Speed comes from two places, faster hardware and smarter organization, and both are now hitting walls (power, wire delay, memory latency). Amdahl's Law then caps what any single improvement can achieve.

Cost drops while performance and capacity climb; a laptop now has the power of a mainframe from 10–15 years ago. Processor speed and memory capacity grew, but memory *speed* lags processor speed. Your note's analogy: an ultra-fast CPU on slow memory is a Ferrari on a mountain road. The bottleneck has moved from processing speed to data movement.

- **Power** rises with clock rate and density.
- **RC delay**: as components shrink, wires get thinner (R up) and closer together (C up), so the RC product and delay go up.
- **Memory latency and throughput** stay behind.

- **Multicore**: several processors on one chip with a large shared cache; more performance without raising the clock.
- **MIC** (Many Integrated Cores): 50+ cores per chip.
- **GPGPU**: the same operation on many data sets at once.

# Chapter 3: A Top-Level View of Computer Function and Interconnection

Slides: `Attachments/Chapter 3 - Top Level View of Function and Interconnnection.pdf`. Stallings 11e. Previous: [[Chapter 2 - Performance Issues]]. All chapters together: [[Cross-Chapter Connections]]. Study aids generated in NotebookLM are in `Attachments/` (Chapter 3 mind map, PCIe video).

## The one idea

A computer works by repeating one loop, fetch an instruction and execute it, and everything else (interrupts, I/O, DMA, buses) is about keeping that loop fed with instructions and data and letting slow devices interrupt it without stalling it. Interconnection is the set of pathways carrying addresses, data, and control between CPU, memory, and I/O; it started as a shared bus and has moved to point-to-point links because a shared bus stops scaling.

## Program concept

Hardwired systems are inflexible. General-purpose hardware can do different jobs if it is given different control signals, so instead of rewiring you supply a new sequence of steps. Each step is an arithmetic or logical operation, and each operation needs its own control signals. The control unit gets a unique code per operation (ADD, MOVE) and a hardware segment turns the code into control signals. Control unit + ALU = CPU; you also need I/O for data in and results out, and main memory for temporary storage. This is the von Neumann model from [[Chapter 1 - Basic Concepts & Computer Evolution]] restated as "what happens per instruction".

## Instruction cycle

**Fetch**: PC holds the address of the next instruction; the processor reads it from memory, increments PC, and loads it into IR. **Execute**, one or a combination of:

- processor-memory: data transfer between CPU and memory
- processor-I/O: data transfer between CPU and an I/O module
- data processing: arithmetic or logic on data
- control: change the sequence, e.g. a jump

The execute cycle can need several memory accesses. Slide example: PDP-11 `ADD B, A` (multiple registers, no single accumulator) does: fetch the instruction, read A into a register, read B into another register, add, write the result to A.

(The hypothetical-machine execution trace and state diagrams on slides 8–10 are images; the IAS registers from Chapter 1, PC/IR/MAR/MBR/AC, are what they animate.)

## Interrupts

A mechanism for other modules (mostly I/O) to break into the normal instruction sequence. Reason: external devices are slower than the processor, and you don't want the CPU idling while the printer works; the device interrupts when it needs attention. Also used to stop a process on an error, recoverable or not.

**Classes**: program (overflow, divide by zero), timer (internal timer; basis of pre-emptive multitasking), I/O (from an I/O controller), hardware failure (power failure, memory parity error).

**Interrupt cycle** (added to the instruction cycle): after execute, check for an interrupt signal. None → fetch next instruction. Pending → suspend the current program, **save context**, set PC to the interrupt handler's start address, run the handler, **restore context**, resume.

**Timing**: with a short I/O wait the interrupt saves little because the processor barely waits anyway; with a long I/O wait it lets the processor run other code during the wait (slides 18–19 show both timelines).

**Multiple interrupts**:

- *Disable* interrupts while one is handled; others stay pending and are checked afterwards. Simple, sequential, ignores urgency.
- *Priorities*: a higher-priority interrupt can interrupt a lower-priority handler (nested); when done, return to the earlier handler.

## I/O and DMA

An I/O module (e.g. a disk controller) exchanges data with the processor using I/O instructions that name a specific device, distinct from memory-referencing instructions. For large transfers it is better to skip the processor: with **direct memory access (DMA)** the processor grants an I/O module authority to read or write memory, and the module issues the memory commands itself, so the transfer doesn't tie up the CPU. (This is the DMA from your Chapter 2 notes.)

## What each unit connects with

| Unit | Receives | Sends |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | data, addresses, control (read, write, timing) | data |
| I/O module | data from computer (output) or peripheral (input), control signals, addresses (e.g. port number) | data to peripheral or computer, control to peripheral (e.g. spin disk), **interrupt signals** |
| CPU | instructions, data, interrupts | data after processing, control signals to other units |

## Buses

A **bus** is a communication pathway connecting two or more devices, usually broadcast, often a group of channels (a 32-bit data bus is 32 one-bit channels). Examples: control/address/data bus (PC), Unibus (DEC PDP).

| Bus | Carries | What its width decides |
|---|---|---|
| Data | data or instructions (indistinguishable at this level) | key determinant of performance (8/16/32/64 bit) |
| Address | source or destination of data | maximum memory capacity, e.g. 8080's 16-bit address bus = 64K address space |
| Control | read/write, interrupt request, clock, timing | (no capacity role; coordinates use of the other two) |

To send data a module must obtain the bus, then transfer; to request data it must obtain the bus, send the request over control and address lines, then wait for the other module to reply.

**Problems with a single bus**: many devices on one bus cause propagation delays; long data paths make coordinating bus use hurt performance; performance collapses as aggregate traffic approaches bus capacity. Fix: multiple buses in a hierarchy (traditional bus architecture, then high-performance bus architecture).

**Bus types**: *dedicated* (separate address and data lines) vs *multiplexed* (shared lines plus a control line saying whether address or data is valid; fewer lines but more complex control).

**Arbitration** (only one module may control the bus at a time, e.g. CPU vs DMA controller): *centralized* (one arbiter/bus controller, part of CPU or separate) vs *distributed* (control logic on every module; each can claim the bus).

**Timing**: *synchronous* (events set by a clock line; one 1-0 is a bus cycle; usually sync on the leading edge; usually one cycle per event) vs *asynchronous* (events depend on the previous event's handshake, no clock; the read and write timing diagrams are images on slides 43–44).

### Problems from the slides (working is mine; slide diagrams weren't readable)

**3.3** 32-bit instructions: first byte opcode, remaining 24 bits an operand or address.

- a) 24 address bits → $2^{24}$ bytes = 16 MB directly addressable.
- b) (i) 32-bit address bus, 16-bit data bus: address is fine in one go, but each 32-bit instruction or operand needs two data-bus transfers, so fetching is about twice as slow as with a 32-bit data bus. - c) PC = 24 bits (holds an address); IR = 8 bits if it holds only the opcode (as in the IAS), 32 if it holds the whole instruction. Depends on the course's IR definition; the IAS one in Chapter 1 is opcode-only.

**3.4** 16-bit address, 16-bit data bus.

- a) 16 address bits → $2^{16}$ = 64K locations; with 16-bit memory that is 64K words (128 KB).
- b) With 8-bit memory it is still 64K addresses, giving 64 KB, and each 16-bit transfer takes two accesses.
- c) A separate I/O address space needs an extra control line distinguishing I/O from memory accesses (memory-mapped I/O avoids it) plus dedicated I/O instructions.
- d) An 8-bit port number gives $2^8$ = 256 8-bit ports; 16-bit ports take two 8-bit port numbers each, so 128.

**3.11** 20 MHz bus clock → 50 ns clock period. The read signal starts to fall in the middle of the second half of T3, i.e. $2\times50 + 37.5 = 137.5$ ns from the start of T1. Allowing 10 ns for settling, data must be on the bus by $137.5 - 10 = 127.5$ ns at the latest. Read-cycle length depends on the timing diagram (a standard read spans T1–T4, so 200 ns); confirm with slide 42, since the slide says some values differ from the book.

## From shared bus to point-to-point

Why the change: electrical constraints when raising the frequency of wide synchronous buses; at higher data rates synchronization and arbitration can't finish in time; multicore chips with lots of on-chip memory made a shared on-chip bus even harder to speed up and keep low-latency. Point-to-point links give lower latency, higher data rate, and better scalability.

### Intel QuickPath Interconnect (QPI, 2008)

Multiple direct pairwise connections (no arbitration), a layered protocol instead of raw control signals, and packetized data with control headers and error-control codes.

| Layer | Job | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Physical | wires and circuitry for sending 1s and 0s | 20-bit **phit** |
| Link | reliable transmission, flow control, error control | 80-bit **flit** = 72-bit payload + 8-bit CRC |
| Routing | direct packets through the fabric; defined by firmware | packet |
| Protocol | high-level rules for exchanging packets, incl. cache coherency | integral number of flits |

Physical port: 84 links; 20 data lanes each way plus a clock lane each way; **differential signaling** (value set by the voltage difference across a wire pair). The physical layer converts 80-bit flits into 20-bit phits by distributing bits round-robin across lanes (multilane distribution).

Link layer: **flow control** stops a sender overrunning the receiver's buffers; **error control** detects and recovers from bit errors (CRC). Protocol layer: cache coherency keeps memory values held in several caches consistent.

### PCI and PCI Express (PCIe)

PCI is a high-bandwidth, processor-independent bus (mezzanine or peripheral). The PCI SIG maintains the specs. **PCIe** is point-to-point and intended to replace bus schemes such as PCI; requirements are high capacity for fast I/O like Gigabit Ethernet and support for time-dependent data streams. Typical layout: a chipset connects processor cores and memory to root PCIe lanes; PCIe **switches** fan out to endpoints, legacy PCI bridges, and slots.

| Layer | Job | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Physical | wires and signalling circuitry | |
| Data link | reliable transmission, flow control; adds error checking and address bits to each TLP | DLLP |
| Transaction | takes read/write requests from software, creates request packets, manages flow between components | TLP |

- **Physical layer**: like QPI but lanes are *bidirectional* and a port has 1, 4, 8, 16, or 32 lanes (the slide says "1, 4, 6, 16, or 32", but 6 looks like a typo for 8; check the spec). Bits go to lanes round-robin; each lane buffers **16 bytes (128 bits)** and encodes them as a **130-bit code word**. No common clock: the receiver syncs on transitions in the data, and the 2 extra bits guarantee transitions even in a long run of 1s.
- **Data link packets**: flow control (rate of TLPs/DLLPs), power management (platform power budgeting), **ACK** (valid packet received), **NAK** (invalid packet; must be resent).
- **Transaction layer**: most transactions are **split**: the source sends a request, frees the link, and waits for a completion. Messages and some writes are **posted** (no response expected). Supports 32-bit and extended 64-bit memory addressing.

- Walk one instruction through fetch, execute, and (if an interrupt is pending) the interrupt cycle, naming PC, IR, MAR, MBR at each step.
- Address bus width vs data bus width: which sets capacity, which sets transfer speed?
- Why does a slow I/O device make interrupts more valuable, not less?
- Name two reasons a shared bus stops scaling and how QPI/PCIe each avoid them.

| Link | reliable transmission, flow control, error control | 80-bit **flit** = 72-bit payload + 8-bit CRC |
| Routing | direct packets through the fabric; defined by firmware | packet |
| Protocol | high-level rules for exchanging packets, incl. cache coherency | integral number of flits |

Physical port: 84 links; 20 data lanes each way plus a clock lane each way; **differential signaling** (value set by the voltage difference across a wire pair). The physical layer converts 80-bit flits into 20-bit phits by distributing bits round-robin across lanes (multilane distribution).

Link layer: **flow control** stops a sender overrunning the receiver's buffers; **error control** detects and recovers from bit errors (CRC). Protocol layer: cache coherency keeps memory values held in several caches consistent.

### PCI and PCI Express (PCIe)

PCI is a high-bandwidth, processor-independent bus (mezzanine or peripheral). The PCI SIG maintains the specs. **PCIe** is point-to-point and intended to replace bus schemes such as PCI; requirements are high capacity for fast I/O like Gigabit Ethernet and support for time-dependent data streams. Typical layout: a chipset connects processor cores and memory to root PCIe lanes; PCIe **switches** fan out to endpoints, legacy PCI bridges, and slots.

| Layer | Job | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Physical | wires and signalling circuitry | |
| Data link | reliable transmission, flow control; adds error checking and address bits to each TLP | DLLP |
| Transaction | takes read/write requests from software, creates request packets, manages flow between components | TLP |

- **Physical layer**: like QPI but lanes are *bidirectional* and a port has 1, 4, 8, 16, or 32 lanes (the slide says "1, 4, 6, 16, or 32", but 6 looks like a typo for 8; check the spec). Bits go to lanes round-robin; each lane buffers **16 bytes (128 bits)** and encodes them as a **130-bit code word**. No common clock: the receiver syncs on transitions in the data, and the 2 extra bits guarantee transitions even in a long run of 1s.
- **Data link packets**: flow control (rate of TLPs/DLLPs), power management (platform power budgeting), **ACK** (valid packet received), **NAK** (invalid packet; must be resent).
- **Transaction layer**: most transactions are **split**: the source sends a request, frees the link, and waits for a completion. Messages and some writes are **posted** (no response expected). Supports 32-bit and extended 64-bit memory addressing.

# Cross-Chapter Connections

Chapters: [[Chapter 1 - Basic Concepts & Computer Evolution]] · [[Chapter 2 - Performance Issues]] · [[Chapter 3 - Function and Interconnection]]

## The whole course in one paragraph

Chapter 1 says what a computer is (stored-program CPU + memory + I/O + interconnect) and how its parts got smaller. Chapter 3 says how it runs (fetch-execute loop, interrupts, buses) and how the parts talk. Chapter 2 says how to judge and improve it, and its main finding is that the bottleneck is no longer the CPU but getting data to it, which is what drives the interconnect changes at the end of Chapter 3.

```
Ch1: parts + history ──► Ch3: how the parts run and talk ──► Ch2: how fast, and what limits it
        ▲                                                            │
        └──────── Moore's Law / multicore / ISA choices ◄────────────┘
```

## Threads that run through all three

**1. The instruction, seen three ways.** One instruction is: an ISA object ([[Chapter 1 - Basic Concepts & Computer Evolution]]: opcode + address, IAS packs two per 40-bit word), a trip through fetch-execute ([[Chapter 3 - Function and Interconnection]]: PC → MAR → memory → MBR → IR → execute), and a cost in cycles ([[Chapter 2 - Performance Issues]]: its CPI). The IAS registers of Ch1 are the machinery that Ch3's instruction cycle animates and Ch2's CPI counts.

**2. Instruction count vs CPI is the RISC/CISC argument in numbers.** Ch1's `A = B + C`: CISC uses 1 instruction, RISC uses 4 (2 loads, add, store). In Ch2's equation $\text{CPU time} = \text{IC}\times\text{CPI}\times T_{\text{cycle}}$, CISC pushes IC down and CPI up, RISC does the opposite. Neither wins by definition; Ch2's code-sequence example (sequence 2 has more instructions but is faster) is the same lesson. Also why "MIPS" as a metric is misleading (a RISC machine can post a higher MIPS figure while doing less work per instruction), while MIPS the ISA is just the RISC teaching machine. Same name, different things.

**3. Address width sets memory size; data width sets speed.** Ch1: IAS has 4096 words because addresses are 12 bits. Ch1: the 80286 raised addressable memory from 1 MB to 16 MB. Ch3: the address bus width determines maximum memory (8080's 16 bits = 64K), the data bus width is a key performance determinant, and Problem 3.3 makes you compute both for a 24-bit address.

**4. The memory/data-movement bottleneck.** Ch2 says memory speed lags the processor and fixes it with wider DRAM, caches, and faster buses. Ch3 is where those buses are defined and where their limits appear (propagation delay, arbitration, capacity). Ch2's MIPS example shows the cost directly: cache misses are 10% of instructions but 0.8 of the 2.24 average CPI. Ch1's x86 history (cache in the 486, prefetch in the 8086) is the same problem attacked chip by chip.

**5. Interconnect evolution.** Ch1's PDP-8 Omnibus is a single shared bus (cheap, flexible, minicomputer-sized). Ch3 shows why a single bus stops working (delays, arbitration, capacity), moves to bus hierarchies, then to point-to-point QPI and PCIe. The trigger the slides give is multicore, which is Ch1's Moore's Law consequence and Ch2's answer to power and RC-delay limits. So: Moore's Law → multicore → shared bus can't keep up → point-to-point.

**6. Multicore's promise and ceiling.** Ch1: multicore = several cores on one chip. Ch2: multicore raises performance without raising the clock, and Amdahl's Law caps it at $1/(1-f)$ speedup for parallel fraction $f$. Ch3: more cores also means more traffic over the interconnect and cache coherency in the QPI protocol layer. Three separate limits on the same design move.

**7. Overlapping slow devices with the CPU.** Ch2 lists DMA as a bus fix for the bottleneck; Ch3 defines it (an I/O module reads/writes memory while the CPU does other work) and interrupts (the device signals when done). Both exist because I/O is far slower than the CPU, and both show up in Ch2's distinction between CPU time (excludes I/O waits) and wall-clock time (includes them).

**8. Layering and packetization as a design habit.** Ch1: ISA as the abstraction between hardware and software. Ch3: QPI/PCIe as physical, link, transaction/protocol layers, each with its own unit (phit/flit/packet, DLLP/TLP). Same reasoning both times: hide implementation behind a stable interface so each side can change independently.

## Quick comparison tables

QPI vs PCIe (both Ch3, both answers to the Ch2 bandwidth problem):

| | QPI | PCIe |
|---|---|---|
| Role | processor-to-processor / chipset | I/O devices (NICs, graphics) |
| Lanes | 20 data lanes each direction, unidirectional pairs | 1–32 bidirectional lanes |
| Encoding | 80-bit flit over 20-bit phits | 128-bit block → 130-bit code word |
| Error handling | 8-bit CRC per flit | ACK/NAK at the data link layer |
| Clocking | clock lane per direction | none; recovered from data transitions |
| Layers | physical, link, routing, protocol | physical, data link, transaction |

Terms that look alike but aren't:

| Pair | Difference |
|---|---|
| Architecture / organization | what the programmer sees / how it is built |
| MIPS (metric) / MIPS (ISA) | instructions per second / a RISC instruction set |
| Response time / throughput | one task's latency / total work per unit time |
| CPU time / wall-clock time | compute only / includes I/O, OS, other programs |
| Synchronous / asynchronous bus | clock-driven / handshake-driven |
| Dedicated / multiplexed bus | separate address and data lines / shared lines plus a validity signal |

## Open questions and slide inconsistencies to resolve

- Moore's Law slide says doubling every year and every 18 months in the same slide.
- PCIe lane counts: slide says "1, 4, 6, 16, or 32" (likely 8, not 6).
- Class IAS exercise: the `JUMP+` logic in your notes looks inverted for `M(5) > 0` (details in Chapter 1 note).
- Slides 8–10, 14–15, 17–23, 37–38, 42–44 (Ch3) and the worked-solution slides in Ch2 are images; I've reproduced the setups and worked the answers myself, so check them against the lecturer's.
